strengths: Originality/significance: The manuscript explores a potentially useful combination of learned optimization and limited-memory rank-one preconditioning. The element-wise neural modules and fixed-length vector buffer are compact and naturally applicable across problem dimensions.

Evaluation: The paper includes both controlled analytic objectives and a real application to human mesh recovery. On 3DPW, the reported PA-MPJPE improves from 55.90 for LGD to 51.58, while the stated parameter count falls from 17.4M to 10.4M.
Efficiency: Runtime and memory measurements are provided. The reported HMR iteration cost is 91 ms and 14.60 GiB for L-SR1, versus 166 ms and 17.81 GiB for LGD.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithm overview, architecture, and major experimental settings are generally readable. The authors also report the recognized runtime limitation rather than concealing it. weaknesses: Soundness—the main theoretical claim is unsupported. Equations (6)–(9) do not implement a projection: the method merely adds a soft secant-residual penalty during meta-training. Consequently, it neither enforces nor guarantees the secant condition, despite repeated claims that the proposed projection does so. Indeed, a PSD matrix satisfying Bq=p can exist only if q^T p is nonnegative, a condition the paper neither assumes nor handles.

Soundness—the derivation and implemented algorithm are inconsistent. Equation (7) defines B as I plus a sum of rank-one matrices, whereas Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 compute the direction using only the rank-one sum. Without the identity term, the matrix is merely PSD and can be highly singular. This discrepancy directly affects both the claimed positive-definite property and reproducibility.

Soundness—even PSD preconditioning does not establish the claimed descent guarantee here. The method applies a learned coordinate-wise step-size vector, so the effective matrix is diag(alpha)B, which need not be symmetric or PSD; therefore g^T diag(alpha)Bg is not guaranteed nonnegative. No convergence or stability result is supplied.

Originality: The method is not an SR1 update in the standard sense: it does not use the signed, secant-satisfying SR1 correction and instead accumulates learned vv^T terms, an approach the paper acknowledges was already used in prior learned optimization work. The main apparent addition is secant-residual regularization, making the novelty substantially narrower than advertised.

Evaluation/significance: The optimization evidence is too limited to support claims of broad effectiveness or convergence to global minima. The performance profile contains only 30 problem/dimension combinations, models are trained on the same three function families used for testing, raw terminal errors are absent, and no results across training seeds or uncertainty estimates are reported. L-BFGS also clearly outperforms L-SR1 in the quadratic experiment.

Evaluation: The HMR result is confined to one test dataset and primarily compared against LGD from 2020. There are no multiple-run statistics, component-matched parameter controls, secant-residual measurements, or tests showing that the purported curvature mechanism—not model capacity or training choices—causes the gain. Selecting the checkpoint on 3DPW validation also weakens the broad no-fine-tuning/generalization language.

Claim inconsistency: The paper repeatedly describes training as self-supervised and requiring no annotated data, but Equation (13) uses ground-truth 3D joints, pose, and shape parameters through ||Theta_k-Theta_gt||_1, obtained from AMASS. This is supervised training with privileged ground-truth body parameters, even if 2D inputs are synthetically projected.

Reproducibility: Code is only promised. Important details are missing, including random seeds, baseline tuning ranges and selection rules, initialization distributions, dropout probabilities, several HMR loss weights, exact stopping/evaluation budgets, and numerical tables underlying the plots. Algorithm/equation inconsistencies further prevent reliable reconstruction.

Presentation: Several conclusions overstate the evidence, including that the method ensures the secant constraint, is positive definite, converges to global minima faster, and consistently outperforms existing optimizers. The paper also alternates between SR1, L-SR1, and LSR1 descriptions while the actual update is materially different from classical SR1.

Limitations/ethics: The limitations section discusses only runtime and omits the absence of theoretical guarantees, dependence on task-specific meta-training, narrow empirical coverage, and supervised AMASS targets. No research-ethics or dataset-governance discussion is provided for human motion and in-the-wild imagery, including privacy, consent/licensing, demographic bias, or downstream misuse. These omissions are not necessarily fatal alone, but the limitations treatment is incomplete.

strengths: The paper explores a useful direction: combining learned optimization with structured low-rank preconditioning. Constructing the preconditioner from buffered outer products is computationally simple, guarantees a PSD matrix before step-size scaling, and permits dimension-agnostic, element-wise neural modules.

The evaluation spans controlled quadratic and benchmark-function experiments as well as human mesh recovery. The ablation comparing training with and without the secant penalty provides some evidence that the penalty improves convergence and alignment with Newton directions.

The HMR results are promising within the narrow set of reported comparisons: L-SR1 improves PA-MPJPE from LGD's 55.90 to 51.74 after four steps (51.58 after thirteen), while using 10.4M rather than 17.4M parameters. The reported per-iteration runtime and memory are also lower than LGD's.

The manuscript is generally organized and includes architecture, hyperparameter, runtime, memory, and qualitative-result appendices. It also honestly identifies higher runtime than first-order methods as a limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim that a learned projection enforces the secant condition is unsupported. Equations 8-9 do not compute a projection or impose the constraint; they merely add a finite-weight soft penalty during meta-training. No theorem, residual bound, or empirical secant-residual measurement shows that the resulting matrices satisfy the condition. The repeated claims that the method 'ensures' or 'maintains' the secant condition are therefore false as stated.

Soundness: Algorithm 1 is inconsistent with the mathematical formulation. Equation 7 defines B_k as B_0 plus the buffered outer products, with B_0 initialized to the identity, whereas Algorithm 1 computes the direction using only the outer-product sum. Its initialization p_0=x_0 and q_0=g_0 also does not match their definitions as iterate and gradient differences.

Soundness: PSD of B_k does not provide the claimed descent guarantee for the implemented update. The algorithm multiplies B_k g by a learned coordinate-wise vector alpha. Although alpha has positive entries, diag(alpha)B_k need not be symmetric or PSD, and g^T diag(alpha)B_k g can be negative. Thus Lemma 1 does not establish descent for Algorithm 1.

Originality: the method is not meaningfully an SR1 update as presented. It neither uses the SR1 residual/denominator update nor enforces its secant equation; it learns vectors whose outer products form a PSD preconditioner, an idea the manuscript itself attributes to prior learned-optimization work. The main apparent novelty is a secant-residual regularizer, not the claimed projection or SR1 construction.

Soundness and claims: the assertion that training requires no annotated data or supervised meta-training is contradicted by the HMR experiment. Equation 13 explicitly includes an L1 loss between predicted variables and ground-truth Theta_gt, and training uses AMASS ground-truth SMPL pose and shape parameters. Likewise, 'without fine-tuning' is misleading because the HMR optimizer is domain-trained for 400K meta-iterations.

Evaluation: the analytic evidence is too limited for the broad optimizer claims. The performance-profile model is trained on the same three function families used in testing, so it demonstrates mainly cross-dimensional generalization rather than generalization to unseen objectives. Results are shown only as plots, with no uncertainty, repeated-run statistics, statistical tests, or detailed per-problem outcomes. Baseline tuning grids and budgets are not reported.

Evaluation and significance: the real-world study contains only one downstream task and compares principally against older optimization-based HMR systems. It does not isolate the effects of the proposed preconditioner, learned coordinate-wise learning rates, initialization module, and supervised training loss. Consequently, the source of the HMR improvement is unclear.

Presentation: several conclusions overstate the evidence, including 'state-of-the-art performance,' 'converging to the global minimum faster,' and seamless applicability to broader optimization frameworks. The quadratic experiment actually shows L-BFGS converging faster, while no general convergence result or broad cross-domain evaluation is supplied. The HMR reconstruction loss is also L1 and therefore does not satisfy the paper's stated twice-differentiable objective assumption.

Reproducibility: code is only promised for future release, and important details are missing, including random seeds and repeat counts, dropout probabilities, exact HMR loss weights, initialization-module training details, baseline hyperparameter search spaces, initial-point distributions, and the test iteration budgets used for the profiles. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the headline experiments.

Limitations and ethics: the limitations section discusses only runtime and overlooks the lack of exact secant enforcement, absence of convergence/descent guarantees, dependence on task-specific supervised meta-training, and narrow empirical coverage. For HMR, there is no discussion of demographic bias, failure cases, privacy implications, or dataset licensing/consent, despite predicting human bodies from imagery. These concerns are not necessarily prohibitive, but they require treatment.

strengths: The paper explores a useful direction: combining learned optimization with a structured, limited-memory low-rank preconditioner. Element-wise shared networks permit application across dimensions, and the resulting optimizer is substantially smaller than LGD (10.4M versus 17.4M parameters).

The empirical results are promising. On 3DPW, L-SR1 improves PA-MPJPE from LGD's 55.90 to 51.74 at the same four-step budget and reaches 51.58 after 13 steps. The appendix also reports lower per-iteration HMR runtime and memory than LGD (91 ms/14.60 GiB versus 166 ms/17.81 GiB).

Ablating the secant penalty is informative: the projected/regularized variant generally improves quadratic convergence and alignment with the Newton direction. The evaluation includes analytic functions, dimension shifts, HMR, computational measurements, and architectural ablations.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually clear. It identifies runtime relative to first-order methods as a limitation, and no major ethical concern arises from the optimization method itself.
weaknesses: The principal soundness claim is incorrect as written. Equations 6–9 do not implement a projection: the network is merely trained with a finite-weight secant-residual penalty. Consequently, Bq=p is neither enforced nor shown empirically to hold, despite repeated claims that the method “satisfies” or “enforces” the secant condition. No residual values, feasibility analysis, or guarantee are provided.

The stated preconditioner and implemented algorithm are inconsistent. Equation 7 defines B=I+sum(vv^T), whereas Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 compute the direction using only sum(vv^T)g. This changes positive definiteness to, at best, semidefiniteness and can produce a zero direction. Moreover, applying coordinate-wise learning rates gives diag(alpha)Bg; even if B is symmetric PSD and alpha is positive, diag(alpha)B need not define a descent direction. Thus the theoretical PSD/descent argument does not establish the property of the actual update.

The structured class B=I+sum(vv^T) is much narrower than the PSD cone invoked in Equation 6. Exact secant satisfaction can be impossible; for example, Bq=p would require q^T p=q^T Bq≥||q||^2. The paper neither recognizes this feasibility restriction nor proves approximation guarantees. The method is also not an SR1 update in the standard sense, since it omits SR1's signed, secant-derived correction and instead accumulates learned PSD outer products already used in prior learned optimization.

The claim of requiring “no annotated data or supervised meta-training” conflicts directly with the HMR experiment. Equation 13 contains ||Theta_k-Theta_gt||_1, and training uses AMASS ground-truth SMPL pose, shape, and 3D joints. Calling this setup self-supervised materially overstates the contribution.

The evidence is too narrow for the broad optimizer and generalization claims. The first quadratic study has only 32 test functions and shifts merely from dimension 2 to 10. The performance profile comprises 30 combinations of only quadratics, Rosenbrock, and Rastrigin, with no repeated-run uncertainty. HMR is the sole real application, and its main table contains only one directly relevant learned-optimizer baseline. Claims of consistently outperforming traditional solvers are unsupported because L-BFGS wins the quadratic experiment and comprehensive time-to-accuracy comparisons are absent.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is only promised, random seeds and initialization distributions are not fully specified, baseline tuning ranges/protocols and several test iteration budgets are omitted, and dropout probabilities are absent from the architecture tables. Most results lack variance over independent training runs.

The limitations section discusses only runtime. It should also address lack of an exact secant guarantee, dependence on task-specific meta-training and labeled AMASS targets, restricted benchmark diversity, possible optimizer instability, and HMR dataset demographic/domain bias. These issues are especially important because the paper makes broad robustness and generalization claims. Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the central theoretical characterization and supervision claim require substantial correction before the work can be reliably built upon.

strengths: The PSD-by-construction limited-memory preconditioner is simple, scalable, and computationally interpretable. Combining learned rank-one vectors with a secant-mismatch regularizer is a reasonable model-based learned-optimization design.

The evaluation includes useful diagnostic ablations beyond endpoint accuracy: Newton-direction alignment, secant residuals, buffer-size sensitivity, dimension transfer, reduced-data training, and runtime/memory measurements.

On 3DPW, L-SR1 improves over LGD at the matched four-step comparison (51.74 vs. 55.90 PA-MPJPE) while reporting lower total runtime (364 vs. 664 ms). The comparison with the no-secant variant also provides evidence that the regularizer contributes to performance.

The manuscript is generally readable and explicitly acknowledges important limitations, including task-distribution dependence, higher per-step cost, limited empirical scope, and the fact that coordinate-wise learning rates invalidate a straightforward PSD-based descent guarantee.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is not well supported. Equation 6 is called a projection, but it minimizes only secant residual and contains no distance to the matrix being projected; its solution is generally non-unique. Equation 8 is merely a restricted secant-fitting problem. Moreover, the implemented update I+sum(vv^T) is not the classical SR1 update, which includes a signed normalization term. Thus the names “Projection-Guided” and “Learned-SR1” overstate the connection to the claimed underlying methods.

PSD of the stored preconditioner does not ensure descent for the actual algorithm because the learned coordinate-wise step-size matrix left-multiplies it. The paper recognizes this but supplies neither a substitute guarantee nor sufficiently broad stability evidence. Consequently, the main claimed structural advantage over unconstrained learned optimizers is substantially weakened.

The broad generalization evidence is unconvincing. Performance-profile models are meta-trained separately on quadratics, Rosenbrock, and Rastrigin and then evaluated on the same three function families; the suite has only 30 dimension/function combinations. The N=2 to N=10 experiment changes dimension but not the objective distribution. These protocols do not support claims of broad applicability to unseen optimization problems.

The claims of requiring “no annotated data” and “no task-specific fine-tuning” conflict with the HMR protocol. Equation 12 directly supervises predictions using ground-truth AMASS pose, shape, and 3D quantities, the optimizer is meta-trained specifically for HMR, and checkpoint selection uses 3DPW validation performance. Calling these synthetic ground-truth signals self-supervision does not remove the supervision.

The empirical comparisons are insufficient for the claimed state of the art. Generic optimization lacks direct comparisons to the cited modern learned optimizers, while HMR primarily compares against the 2020 LGD method and LBFGS. Fixed-step comparisons ignore differing per-step costs, baseline tuning grids are not reported, and no parameter-matched learned baseline isolates whether gains arise from curvature structure rather than architecture or capacity.

The key HMR advantage over the matched no-secant ablation is only 1.06 mm at four steps, but results provide no variation across training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. Likewise, the primary performance profile lacks uncertainty or repeated initializations, making robustness difficult to assess.

Appendix B.2 substantially complicates the design justification: scalarized learning rates perform dramatically better on the controlled quadratics, whereas the vector version gains only 0.22 mm on 3DPW without uncertainty estimates. Reported quantities are also inconsistently described as AUC in the main text and mean inner loss in Table 3, and secant weights/settings differ across sections without a sufficiently clear mapping.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite considerable implementation detail: the code/project footnote is empty, and important items such as dropout rates, HMR loss weights, complete baseline hyperparameter grids, initialization distributions, evaluation horizons, and seeds for principal results are missing.

Originality and significance are limited by the fact that PSD outer-product learned preconditioners already appear in cited work; the main addition is a secant penalty. With evidence restricted to closely matched analytic families and one HMR pipeline, the manuscript does not yet demonstrate that this incremental mechanism is a generally useful learned optimizer.

The impact statement is perfunctory. For an HMR application, the paper should discuss privacy, demographic/pose-distribution bias, and possible disparate accuracy arising from AMASS and 3DPW, even if no severe ethical issue is apparent.

strengths: The manuscript is well organized and visually readable, with a clear algorithmic description and an honest limitations section.

The limited-memory PSD parameterization is computationally practical: buffered rank-one products avoid materializing a dense matrix, while shared element-wise modules permit application at unseen dimensions.

The evaluation includes useful diagnostics beyond final loss, including Newton-direction alignment, buffer-size sweeps, a no-secant ablation, runtime/memory measurements, and test-time secant residuals.

On 3DPW, the reported 4-step result improves PA-MPJPE over LGD from 55.90 to 51.74 while reducing reported runtime from 664 ms to 364 ms. The no-secant variant obtains 52.80, suggesting some benefit from secant regularization.
The authors appropriately acknowledge task-distribution dependence, unrolled-training cost, higher per-step cost than first-order methods, and added hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The main quasi-Newton justification is weaker than claimed. Equation (6) is called a PSD projection, but it minimizes only secant mismatch and contains no distance to the original matrix; it is generally non-unique. Equation (8) is not solved as a projection either—the mismatch is simply used as a training regularizer. PGSM is therefore more accurately characterized as PSD parameterization with secant regularization.

PSD does not ensure descent for the implemented update because coordinate-wise learning rates left-multiply the preconditioner, making the effective operator nonsymmetric. The paper acknowledges this but supplies neither a replacement guarantee nor empirical measurements of descent failures. Even in the scalar case, semidefiniteness guarantees non-ascent rather than necessarily strict descent, contrary to Lemma F.1's wording.

The method is not an SR1 update in the standard technical sense. Classical SR1 uses a signed, normalized residual outer product with a curvature denominator; L-SR1 learns arbitrary vectors and adds only positive outer products. Its matrix is restricted to I plus a PSD low-rank term, so its eigenvalues cannot fall below one. The connection to SR1 is largely inspirational, while learned low-rank PSD preconditioning is already present in cited prior work.

Exact PSD secant consistency requires p^Tq >= 0, which need not hold for the non-convex HMR objective. The paper does not analyze incompatible secant pairs or report their frequency. Moreover, normalizing quadratic Hessians to unit Frobenius norm makes their inverse eigenvalues at least one, unusually favoring the restricted I-plus-PSD parameterization.

The analytic evidence is narrow and partly in-distribution. Performance-profile models are separately trained on the same three function families used for testing, across only 30 family/dimension combinations. The aggregate plot lacks per-problem results, uncertainty, failure counts, and a clearly specified test iteration budget, so it cannot substantiate broad optimizer-generalization claims.

The HMR evaluation compares principally with LGD, LBFGS, and the authors' ablation, reports only PA-MPJPE, and provides no multi-seed uncertainty or statistical analysis. Consequently, the roughly 1.2 mm improvement over the matched no-secant model has uncertain robustness. Comparisons with regression systems are not controlled because their data, inputs, and objectives differ.

Claims of requiring no annotated data or task-specific fine-tuning contradict the protocol. The optimizer is trained for 400K iterations specifically on AMASS, and Equation (12) explicitly uses ground-truth pose, shape, and 3D-joint quantities. Labeling these signals self-supervised does not remove the supervision, materially overstating data efficiency and task generality.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The project/code footnote has no usable link, and important details are missing or ambiguous, including lambda_2D and lambda_self, dropout rates, benchmark initialization domains, baseline tuning grids and selected hyperparameters, precise test budgets, and random seeds. The quantity reported as AUC in the main text around 3.07/7.33 is also described as mean inner loss in Table 3.

The presentation repeatedly overstates what is established through terms such as “projection,” “second-order,” “self-supervised,” “state-of-the-art,” and broad applicability. The limitations section does not address the supervision contradiction, restricted preconditioner expressivity, or absence of a descent guarantee for the actual update.

The ethics discussion is boilerplate despite plausible privacy, surveillance, and demographic/body-shape bias concerns in human mesh recovery. There is no discussion of dataset consent, licensing, representativeness, subgroup performance, or misuse. These concerns may be manageable but deserve appropriate treatment.

strengths: Soundness: The PSD-by-construction preconditioner is clearly specified, computationally tractable, and accompanied by an appropriately cautious acknowledgment that coordinate-wise learning rates remove any general descent guarantee. The controlled quadratic results show that the secant penalty improves convergence and Newton-direction alignment over the matched no-penalty ablation.

Evaluation: The paper examines several relevant dimensions—optimization trajectories, dimension transfer, buffer size, secant residuals, runtime/memory, data efficiency, and a non-convex HMR application. On 3DPW, L-SR1 improves PA-MPJPE over LGD from 55.90 to 51.74 in four steps while reducing reported runtime from 664 ms to 364 ms.

Significance: Reducing the number of iterations is practically useful for inverse problems such as HMR, where evaluating each objective is expensive. The limited-memory construction and coordinate-shared modules also make the approach applicable across dimensionalities.

Originality: Combining learned rank-one preconditioning, a limited-memory buffer, PSD structure, and a secant-residual meta-training objective is a coherent and reasonably novel model-based learned-optimization contribution, even though its ingredients have close precedents.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized and unusually transparent about the lack of a descent guarantee, task-dependent per-step tradeoffs, meta-training costs, and limited empirical scope. Figures and algorithms make the update easy to follow.
weaknesses: Soundness: PGSM is described as a projection, but Eq. (6) is only a secant-residual minimization over PSD matrices—not a projection of a given matrix under a matrix norm—and can be non-unique. Eq. (8) further restricts the matrix to I plus PSD rank-one terms, which is substantially narrower than the PSD cone. The terminology and theoretical interpretation should therefore be weakened or formalized.

The connection to classical SR1 is limited. Classical SR1 uses a signed, residual-dependent correction divided by a curvature term, whereas L-SR1 accumulates learned positive outer products. Since the element-wise step-size vector can also destroy descent, the method currently has neither the defining SR1 secant property nor a convergence/descent result; its support is principally empirical.

The performance-profile evidence is not sufficiently controlled for a strong general-optimizer claim. Learned models are meta-trained on the same three objective families used in the 30-problem evaluation, apparently with function-specific hyperparameters, while generic baselines receive incompletely documented tuning. Results are reported only as an aggregate profile, without raw per-problem outcomes, seed variation, or uncertainty, and a fixed iteration budget does not account for differing per-step costs.

The claimed generalization remains narrow: quadratic transfer is only from dimension 2 to 10, while the larger 50–1000-dimensional benchmark changes dimension but not objective family. HMR is the sole real application and the principal learned baseline is from 2020. Multiple downstream problems or transfer to genuinely unseen objective families would make the broad applicability claim substantially more convincing.

The HMR evidence lacks repeated-training uncertainty or statistical analysis. The comparison with the no-secant variant is useful, but it does not isolate whether improvements arise specifically from better curvature estimation rather than regularization of meta-training. The scalar-rate ablation also shows substantially better quadratic loss than the selected vector-rate model, complicating the general optimizer narrative.

Several claims are overstated or ambiguous. The optimizer is called self-supervised and said to require no annotated data or task-specific fine-tuning, yet the HMR meta-loss directly uses AMASS ground-truth pose, shape, and 3D quantities, and the optimizer is meta-trained for 400K iterations specifically on the HMR pipeline. It is accurate to say that it needs no 3DPW fine-tuning, but not that it avoids task-specific training or supervision altogether.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code/project footnote contains no usable link; baseline search spaces, several test budgets and initialization details, HMR loss weights, dropout settings, and seed-level HMR results are absent. The reported algorithm and main training hyperparameters are helpful but insufficient to reproduce the central comparisons reliably.

Ethics and limitations: The limitations appendix is candid and should be credited, but the impact statement is boilerplate. Because the application estimates human bodies from imagery and relies on aggregated human-motion datasets, the paper should briefly discuss privacy, demographic/domain bias, consent or licensing constraints, and possible surveillance misuse. These concerns do not appear fatal, but they are currently untreated.
